{{Refimprove|date=October 2012}}

In [[physics]], the '''Green's function (or [[fundamental solution]]) for the Laplacian (or Laplace operator) in three variables''' is used to describe the response of a particular type of physical system to a [[point source]]. In particular, this [[Green's function]] arises in systems that can be described by [[Poisson's equation]], a [[partial differential equation]] (PDE) of the form
<math display="block"> \nabla^2 u(\mathbf{x}) = f(\mathbf{x}) </math>
where <math>\nabla^2</math> is the [[Laplace operator]] in <math>\mathbb{R}^3</math>, <math>f(\mathbf{x})</math> is the source term of the system, and <math>u(\mathbf{x})</math> is the solution to the equation. Because <math>\nabla^2</math> is a linear [[differential operator]], the solution <math>u(\mathbf{x})</math> to a general system of this type can be written as an integral over a distribution of source given by <math>f(\mathbf{x})</math>:
<math display="block"> u(\mathbf{x}) = \int G(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{x'})f(\mathbf{x'})d\mathbf{x}'</math>
where the [[Green's function]] for Laplacian in three variables <math>G(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{x'})</math> describes the response of the system at the point <math>\mathbf{x}</math> to a point source located at <math>\mathbf{x'}</math>:
<math display="block">\nabla^2 G(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{x'}) = \delta(\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{x'})</math>
and the point source is given by <math>\delta(\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{x'})</math>, the [[Dirac delta function]].

==Motivation==
One physical system of this type is a charge distribution in [[electrostatics]]. In such a system, the electric field is expressed as the negative gradient of the [[electric potential]], and [[Gauss's law]] in [[differential form]] applies:
<math display="block">\begin{align}
\mathbf{E} &= - \mathbf{\nabla} \phi(\mathbf{x}) \\[1ex]
\boldsymbol{\nabla} \cdot \mathbf{E} &= \frac{\rho(\mathbf{x})}{\varepsilon_0}
\end{align} </math>

Combining these expressions gives us [[Poisson's equation]]:
<math display="block">-\mathbf{\nabla}^2 \phi(\mathbf{x}) = \frac{\rho(\mathbf{x})}{\varepsilon_0} </math>

We can find the solution <math>\phi(\mathbf{x})</math> to this equation for an arbitrary charge distribution by first considering the distribution created by a point charge <math>q</math> located at <math>\mathbf{x'}</math>:
<math display="block">\rho(\mathbf{x}) = q \, \delta(\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{x'})</math>

In this case,
<math display="block">-\frac{\varepsilon_0}{q} \mathbf{\nabla}^2\phi(\mathbf{x}) = \delta(\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{x'}) </math>
which shows that <math>G(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{x'})</math> for <math display="inline">-\frac{\varepsilon_0}{q} \nabla^2</math> will give the response of the system to the point charge <math>q</math>. Then, by linearity of the Laplace operator, we can express <math>\phi(\mathbf{x})</math> as a superposition:
<math display="block"> \phi(\mathbf{x}) = \int G(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{x'}) \rho(\mathbf{x'}) \,d\mathbf{x}'</math>
for a general charge distribution <math>\rho(\mathbf{x})</math>.

==Mathematical exposition==
The free-space [[Green's function]] for the [[Laplace operator]] in three variables is given in terms of the reciprocal distance between two points and is known as the "[[Newton kernel]]" or "[[Newtonian potential]]".  That is to say, the solution of the equation
<math display="block"> \nabla^2 G(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{x'}) = \delta(\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{x'})</math>
is
<math display="block"> G(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{x'}) = -\frac{1}{4\pi \left|\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{x'}\right|},</math>
where <math>\mathbf{x}=(x,y,z)</math> are the standard Cartesian coordinates in a three-dimensional space, and <math>\delta</math> is the [[Dirac delta function]].

The ''algebraic expression'' of the Green's function for the three-variable Laplace operator, apart from the constant term <math>-1/(4\pi)</math> expressed in [[Cartesian coordinates]] shall be referred to as
<math display="block">\frac{1}{|\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{x'}|}
= \left[\left(x - x'\right)^2 + \left(y - y'\right)^2 + \left(z - z'\right)^2\right]^{-{1}/{2}}.
</math>

Many expansion formulas are possible, given the algebraic expression for the Green's function. One of the most well-known of these, the [[Laplace expansion (potential)|Laplace expansion]] for the three-variable Laplace equation, is given in terms of the [[Legendre polynomials#Applications of Legendre polynomials in physics|generating function]] for [[Legendre polynomials]],
<math display="block">  \frac{1}{|\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{x'}|} = \sum_{l=0}^\infty \frac{r_<^l}{r_>^{l+1}} P_l(\cos\gamma),</math>
which has been written in terms of spherical coordinates <math>(r,\theta,\varphi)</math>. The less than (greater than) notation means, take the primed or unprimed spherical radius depending on which is less than (greater than) the other. The <math>\gamma</math> represents the angle between the two arbitrary vectors <math>(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{x'})</math> given by
<math display="block">\cos\gamma = \cos\theta\cos\theta' + \sin\theta\sin\theta' \cos(\varphi-\varphi').</math>

The free-space circular cylindrical Green's function (see below) is given in terms of the reciprocal distance between two points. The expression is derived in Jackson's ''Classical Electrodynamics''.<ref>{{cite book | last = Jackson | title = Classical Electrodynamics | edition = 3rd | pages = 125–127}}</ref> Using the Green's function for the three-variable Laplace operator, one can integrate the [[Poisson equation]] in order to determine the potential function.  Green's functions can be expanded in terms of the basis elements (harmonic functions) which are determined using the separable [[coordinate systems]] for the [[linear partial differential equation]].  There are many expansions in terms of special functions for the Green's function.  In the case of a boundary put at infinity with the boundary condition setting the solution to zero at infinity, then one has an infinite-extent Green's function.  For the three-variable Laplace operator, one can for instance expand it in the rotationally invariant coordinate systems which allow [[separation of variables]].  For instance:
<math display="block">  \frac{1}{|\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{x'}|} =
\frac{1}{\pi\sqrt{R R'}}
\sum_{m=-\infty}^\infty e^{im(\varphi-\varphi')} Q_{m-\frac{1}{2}}(\chi)</math>
where
<math display="block"> \chi = \frac{R^2 + {R'}^2 + \left(z-z'\right)^2}{2RR'}</math>
and <math>Q_{m-\frac{1}{2}}(\chi)</math> is the odd-half-integer degree [[Legendre function]] of the second kind, which is a toroidal harmonic.  Here the expansion has been written in terms of cylindrical coordinates <math>(R,\varphi,z)</math>.  See for instance [[Toroidal coordinates]].

Using one of the [[Whipple formulae]] for toroidal harmonics we can obtain an alternative form of the Green's function
<math display="block">\frac{1}{|\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{x'}|} =
\sqrt{\frac{\pi}{2RR'(\chi^2-1)^{1/2}}}
\sum_{m=-\infty}^\infty \frac{\left(-1\right)^m}{\Gamma(m+1/2)}  P_{-\frac{1}{2}}^m
{\left(\frac{\chi}{\sqrt{\chi^2-1}}\right)} e^{im(\varphi-\varphi')}</math>
in terms for a toroidal harmonic of the first kind.

The above expressions for the Green's function for the three-variable Laplace operator are examples of single summation expressions for this Green's function.  There are also single-integral expressions for this Green's function.  Examples of these can be seen to exist in rotational cylindrical coordinates as an integral [[Laplace transform]] in the difference of vertical heights whose kernel is given in terms of the order-zero Bessel function of the first kind as
<math display="block">  \frac{1}{|\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{x'}|} =
\int_0^\infty J_0{\left( k\sqrt{R^2 + {R'}^2 - 2RR'\cos(\varphi-\varphi')}\right)} e^{-k(z_>-z_<)}\,dk,</math>
where <math>z_> (z_<)</math> are the greater (lesser) variables <math>z</math> and <math>z'</math>.
Similarly, the Green's function for the three-variable Laplace equation can be given as a Fourier integral [[cosine transform]] of the difference of vertical heights whose kernel is given in terms of the order-zero modified Bessel function of the second kind as
<math display="block">  \frac{1}{|\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{x'}|} =
\frac{2}{\pi} \int_0^\infty K_0{\left( k\sqrt{R^2 + {R'}^2 - 2RR'\cos(\varphi-\varphi')} \right)} \cos[k(z-z')] \, dk. </math>

==Rotationally invariant Green's functions for the three-variable Laplace operator==
Green's function expansions exist in all of the rotationally invariant coordinate systems which are known to yield solutions to the three-variable Laplace equation through the separation of variables technique.
{{div col|colwidth=25em}}
* [[cylindrical coordinates]]
* [[spherical coordinates]]
* [[Prolate spheroidal coordinates]]
* [[Oblate spheroidal coordinates]]
* [[Parabolic coordinates]]
* [[Toroidal coordinates]]
* [[Bispherical coordinates]]
* [[Flat-ring cyclide coordinates]]
* [[Flat-disk cyclide coordinates]]
* [[Bi-cyclide coordinates]]
* [[Cap-cyclide coordinates]]
{{div col end}}
